title: One minute, no notes
summary: Impromptu week: a slip comes out of the summit pouch, you get thirty seconds to think and one minute to talk, and stopping is the only way to lose. Then argue the motion the ledger has been walking toward all week.
materials: the summit pouch and a dozen blank slips
an index card and a pencil, for three words and no more
a grown up to draw the slips, hold the timer and take the other side
your ledger page and the three column decision sheet from Build

steps.title: Thirty seconds to think, one minute to talk
steps.body:
Every speech you have given this season was written first. Today none of them are. A folded slip comes out of the pouch, you read it out loud, you get thirty seconds, and then you talk for a whole minute standing up. That is the entire format.

The fear is going blank, so you get a shape to fall into when you do. Four moves, in this order. Say your one point in a single sentence. Say why you think it. Give one example, from your own life if you have one, because you always have one. Then say what it means for anybody listening. Point, reason, example, meaning. That shape will carry a minute on almost any slip in the pouch, including the silly ones, and knowing it is there is what stops the blank from arriving in the first place.

The thirty seconds are for choosing, not for writing. Three words on the card, maximum. If you write sentences you will read them, and reading is not what this is.

Now the two rules that matter more than the shape.

The first: silence beats um. When you lose your thread, stop talking and count one, two in your head. A listener hears a pause as somebody thinking. A listener hears um as somebody drowning, and the strange part is that the pause feels enormous to you and lasts no time at all to them. Practise the pause on purpose today, at least once in every minute, even when you do not need it.

The second: laughing is allowed, stopping is not. If the slip is ridiculous, say so and keep going. If you contradict yourself halfway, say that too and keep going. The minute is the job. Sitting down at forty seconds is the only real failure here, and the timer is the referee both of you share, so it is not on your side and it is not against you.

This week's question is the one the money has been walking toward since week 5, and the last slip in the pouch is going to be exactly it. Every yes is a quiet no to something else. What did this season's yes cost you? You said yes to a shop. That yes ate afternoons, weekends, a bench and about fifteen hours you will not get back. Name what those hours would have been. Do not soften it, and do not pretend the answer is nothing, because a choice that cost nothing was never a choice.

steps.title: Fill the pouch, then empty it
steps.body:
First, fill it. Write ten slips, fold them and drop them in. Four should be silly, four should be real, and two should be about this spring. Silly ones like the best sandwich is not the one you think, or every house should have one useless room. Real ones like the thing I changed my mind about this year, or what a person owes somebody who lends them money. Spring ones like the worst hour of Market Day, or what I would tell somebody opening a stand next Saturday. You write all ten, which means you cannot know which one is coming, only that you wrote it.

Then empty it. A grown up shakes the pouch, draws one and hands it over. You read it out loud, turn the timer, take your thirty seconds with the card, and go.

Three rounds, all standing, all recorded. After each one the grown up says exactly two things and nothing else: one thing that worked, and one thing to change in the next round. No rescuing mid speech, no matter how long the pause gets.

Between rounds, one job for you. Say out loud which of the four moves you actually used, and which you skipped. Most people skip the example under pressure, and the example is the only part a listener remembers a day later.

The third round is not drawn from the pouch. The third slip is this week's question, handed to you: every yes is a quiet no to something else, so what did this season's yes cost you? Same thirty seconds, same minute, same rule about stopping.
checklist: Ten slips are written and folded, and I wrote all of them myself
Three whole minutes were delivered standing, with the timer running and nobody rescuing me
Nothing longer than three words went on the card in the thinking time
I used a deliberate pause instead of an um at least once in each minute
After each round I named which of the four moves I used and which I skipped

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record at least two of the three impromptu minutes, including the last one, with the timer where the camera can see or hear it, and do not stop recording during a pause. Then, still on camera, answer this week's question in your own words with the decision sheet in your hand: every yes is a quiet no to something else, so what did this season's yes cost you? Name one real thing you gave up, and say whether you would say yes again knowing that.
